Miracle Baby

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Baby survives 12 resuscitation in 24 hours

Unique Selling Point:
Surviving 12 resuscitations is unheard of. The more you have, the more unlikely you will survive the event, and the more likely there will be severe neurological fallout.
At all points in time, they had to counsel parents that outcome was dismal. Micro-cephalic spastic CP child. Need to stop interventions, turn everything off. If had one or two resuscitations, chance of CP is about 80% - 12 means about 100%. Parents didn’t lose hope or faith, refused to sign forms.
Worldwide after one cardiac arrest chance of survival is 30%. Don’t keep track after that. Probably halves after that on each subsequent resuscitation. Will check up on numbers and ask cardiologist (he is head of resuscitation council of SA).
The team believed he was braindead. They even thought it was unethical to keep resuscitating him, because he would have no quality of life. However, the parents were the ones who had to make that decision and refused.
About four weeks later, despite everything, off ventilator. Went to rehab. This is October last year. Now making neurological recovery. Not normal – expected – but able to talk, clap, crawl.
Some things might be permanent – intellectual capacity might be impaired. Will be able to communicate, walk and talk.


Summary:
Dr Ashley Jeeverathnum is a specialist pulmonologist at Netcare Alberton, who says he has never seen anything like this.
In around November 2022 a two-year-old was brought to the hospital with a volvulus: a condition in which the intestine wraps around itself, cuts off blood supply and dies. It’s a relatively common condition, usually caused by congenital abnormalities (the bowel is too long or too loose in abdomen, the vasculature abnormal). It is resolved by surgery to remove the dead part of the bowel.
The child was very ill: because the blood supply was cut off and intestine was gangrenous – lots of bacterial translocation into blood stream. Very septic. Organisms from gut in blood stream. Respiratory failure, shock, sepsis. He needed initial resuscitation and then surgery.
His initial prognosis was that the degree of respiratory or metabolic failure was incompatible with life. The ICU team ventilated him, fluid resuscitation, isotropes to get blood pressure up to make surgery safer. He was considered safe enough to undergo surgery, taken into theatre… and had his first flatline and cardiac resuscitation in theatre. That was Friday evening.
From that point on Friday evening, the child died 12 times in 24 hours. He had another 12 bouts of active resuscitation for 30-45 minutes every time.
Eventually he stopped flatlining. Then the team figured out he had an abnormal cardiac rhythm in keeping with multi-system inflammatory syndrome (MIC) associated with COVID. Clearly he had had a previous infection. They got a cardiologist involved who helped with rhythm. Then had to oscillate him – higher form of ventilation. Amount of fluid: fluid overload. All organs started failing. Had to put him on dialysis. Remove some of the fluid from lungs to ventilate him.


Further information:
Doesn’t know if it’s world first but in 15 years of experience as medical doctor, has never seen something like that. Usually after three resus everyone gives up.
Out of rehab, at home. He doesn’t swallow well – has to be fed by stomach tube. Doesn’t have coordination yet. Crawling, two-word sentences, hum rhymes. Three but behaves like a one to two year old
When he left hospital to go to rehab, thought he was blind and deaf. Could not move any limbs. Completely paralysed, fed by stomach tube. Tracheostomy.
In hospital for a month or two. Rehab for four months.
Speaks of strength of ICU team and faith of parents. Positive outcome. Feels unfair to keep resuscitating with dismal outcome.
Factors for success: extreme youth. But good neurological outcome speaks to efficiency of resuscitation – supplying blood to brain and rest of the body. Very active (brutal) process – taking over function of the heart.

Script: Laura and Matthew Botha tried for 12 years to have a child, eventually, opting for adoption, but that wasn't so easy, for another two long years - they waited for that call.
.

And the social workers actually named him Quinn. So it was. Yeah, it was just amazing. Unbelievable. . He was made for us in in every way.

C4297 00:02:58:11 - Mathew: It was quite a shock at first to get the call and then to get him here. It was a learning process, ….. But yeah, it was it was just really amazing. C4383 00:00:21:23 Dave: He had several rhythms, ……This particular rhythm is incredibly rare and shouldn't shouldn't appear just…..after bowel operation 00:00:53:21 And in fact it was masked
Script: In other words, among 8 different heart rhythms, critical information was being hidden. The culprits were antibodies from an earlier Covid infection, complicating his treatment and causing his heart to race over 300 beats per minute."

00:02:24:21 -Dave: Usually you have warning signs. You can see a child deteriorate slowly. But with him his were sudden changes which also made managing him quite difficult.

00:03:32:09 - Ashley: because he was so critically ill, he actually flatlined ….about 12 times in the 24 hours that I was looking after him. And each and every point in time, together with the ICU team, we got him back..,

Script: And each time his heart stopped it took over 30 minutes to bring him back to life
00:04:12:22 Erin: what is it like to revive such a small patient?
00:04:19:16 -Ashley: So it's very stressful. There's a lot of hype in the room ……because time is essentially brain. And the more time that you don't have enough cardiac output, the more loss of brain tissue ……will ensue.

Script: It was a miracle but it was costing Mateo - each time he returned it was with less brain function.

Ashley 00:11:04:11So at resuscitation number 9 or 10 ….. you doubt yourself. What are you actually doing. What is the quality of life for this child actually going to be like……, what is the burden going to be like to the parents?

Script: But in that moment - it was about saving his life. ICU Sister Cebile Mbongwa’s 28 years of experience carried her team

00:04:24:00 It becomes difficult when we try to do this and it doesn't work. ……. But what we have learned over the time that we are working with the sick babies never to give up.

Ashley “.we looked at the hope that the parents had and the fact that they didn't want to let go. And we kept going as well.

Script: But the ethical dilemma weight heavily on them

-00:07:43:03 - Dave: when we did the MRI scan of his brain, we saw that there was significant damage. 00:08:17:11 we were saying to them, guys, I'm not so sure, I'm not so sure. 00:08:17:13 And I know how how precious he is to you…... it was it was tough. It was one of the toughest times I've ever had.

00:33:50:12 Laura:…... this angel that we had waited for. And finally we had become parents, and he was everything. And and to be going through that. Yeah. It was. Yeah a nightmare.

00:47:35:02 Erin: So what for you was the miracle moment.

Laura 00:47:49:22 - : when he was still in ICU and he was sleeping, but he started to smile…..and I thought he is coming back.

BREATH

00:38:02:20 - Laura: you had to mourn the baby he was wasn't exactly the same. But it wasn't like he was, you know, when he went into ICU. So that was hard as well.

Script: His brain is young- and able learn new pathways

Matteo mooo

The best part of the day for all of them is physiotherapy with Nansie Grobler

.

Script: It's been a gruelling year, but this festive season - looks promising

00:38:52:03 - Laura: it's just going to get better and better. .. Soon he's going to be walking and running and yeah, we're going to be running off after him again


Script: Matteo recovery has exceeded the medical teams wildest expectations

00:09:18:22 Dave: to then have this with this condition that was completely unusual. I mean, it didn't follow any textbook. Nothing that we've done before, you know, to then have this outcome is is amazing.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Surviving 12 resuscitations is unheard of. The more you have, the more unlikely you will survive the event, and the more likely there will be severe neurological fallout. At all points in time, they had to counsel parents that outcome was dismal. Micro-cephalic spastic CP child. Need to stop interventions, turn everything off. If had one or two resuscitations, chance of CP is about 80% - 12 means about 100%. Parents didn’t lose hope or faith, refused to sign forms. Worldwide after one cardiac arrest chance of survival is 30%. Don’t keep track after that. Probably halves after that on each subsequent resuscitation. Will check up on numbers and ask cardiologist (he is head of resuscitation council of SA). The team believed he was braindead. They even thought it was unethical to keep resuscitating him, because he would have no quality of life. However, the parents were the ones who had to make that decision and refused. About four weeks later, despite everything, off ventilator. Went to rehab. This is October last year. Now making neurological recovery. Not normal – expected – but able to talk, clap, crawl. Some things might be permanent – intellectual capacity might be impaired. Will be able to communicate, walk and talk.
metadata.Summary: Dr Ashley Jeeverathnum is a specialist pulmonologist at Netcare Alberton, who says he has never seen anything like this. In around November 2022 a two-year-old was brought to the hospital with a volvulus: a condition in which the intestine wraps around itself, cuts off blood supply and dies. It’s a relatively common condition, usually caused by congenital abnormalities (the bowel is too long or too loose in abdomen, the vasculature abnormal). It is resolved by surgery to remove the dead part of the bowel. The child was very ill: because the blood supply was cut off and intestine was gangrenous – lots of bacterial translocation into blood stream. Very septic. Organisms from gut in blood stream. Respiratory failure, shock, sepsis. He needed initial resuscitation and then surgery. His initial prognosis was that the degree of respiratory or metabolic failure was incompatible with life. The ICU team ventilated him, fluid resuscitation, isotropes to get blood pressure up to make surgery safer. He was considered safe enough to undergo surgery, taken into theatre… and had his first flatline and cardiac resuscitation in theatre. That was Friday evening. From that point on Friday evening, the child died 12 times in 24 hours. He had another 12 bouts of active resuscitation for 30-45 minutes every time. Eventually he stopped flatlining. Then the team figured out he had an abnormal cardiac rhythm in keeping with multi-system inflammatory syndrome (MIC) associated with COVID. Clearly he had had a previous infection. They got a cardiologist involved who helped with rhythm. Then had to oscillate him – higher form of ventilation. Amount of fluid: fluid overload. All organs started failing. Had to put him on dialysis. Remove some of the fluid from lungs to ventilate him.
metadata.Further information: Doesn’t know if it’s world first but in 15 years of experience as medical doctor, has never seen something like that. Usually after three resus everyone gives up. Out of rehab, at home. He doesn’t swallow well – has to be fed by stomach tube. Doesn’t have coordination yet. Crawling, two-word sentences, hum rhymes. Three but behaves like a one to two year old When he left hospital to go to rehab, thought he was blind and deaf. Could not move any limbs. Completely paralysed, fed by stomach tube. Tracheostomy. In hospital for a month or two. Rehab for four months. Speaks of strength of ICU team and faith of parents. Positive outcome. Feels unfair to keep resuscitating with dismal outcome. Factors for success: extreme youth. But good neurological outcome speaks to efficiency of resuscitation – supplying blood to brain and rest of the body. Very active (brutal) process – taking over function of the heart.
